newsitem.title: UK: Dollar holds firm into European close.
newsitem.headline: Dollar holds firm into European close.

text.p: The dollar ended little changed against the German mark here compared with Wednesday's close as traders and investors remained bullish while assessing the likely reaction of central banks to any renewed push higher.

Another attempt at the new 34-month high at 1.6935 marks was thwarted earlier by Bundesbank vice-president Johann Wilhelm Gaddum. He reiterated the central bank line that it was not in its interests to have the dollar rising "further and further."

Yet, while this added some jitters about an official response to renewed dollar gains, analysts said that it was only likely to be a minor delay to the next move higher. "While day traders are understandably a little worried about the threat of intervention, longer-term players are not being scared as easily because they don't belive either Germany or Japan will back it up with interest rate increases," said Paul Meggyesi, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "The market will eventually try to call their bluff and the Bundesbank needs to play it very carefully because we may find the emperor has no clothes," said Meggyesi. At 1635 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6860/65 marks, little changed from 1.6861/66 at Wednesday's close here in Europe. Against the yen, the dollar was a little higher at 124.24/34 compared with 123.82/92 late Wednesday.

Traders dismissed scattered rumours late in the European session that the Bank of England had sold dollar/yen on behalf of the Bank of Japan. They said nervousness ahead of the psychological 125-yen level and activity in sterling/yen at UK clearing banks were probably behind the rumours.

"It is interesting that despite these rumours doing the rounds the dollar continued to hold up well and shows how comfortable people are with the bullish position," said Eddie Tofpik, trader at MeesPierson Derivatives. The big issue for the market is whether the recent statements from the Bundesbank and Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) are aimed at simply reducing volatility or whether there is a threshold beyond which the central banks will act. Many analysts believe dollar appreciation at an orderly pace will be tolerated and will have a minimal inflationary impact.

They argue, for example, the dollar is only about 10 percent of the mark's trade-weighted basket of currencies, based on U.S. trade with Germany, while the European currencies which together represent almost 60 percent of that basket have shown no net gains against the mark at all this year.
Moreover, concerns about the net inflation impact of dollar-denominated oil imports is offset this year by a drop of more than 20 percent in the oil price since December.

"As far as we can make out, the concerns about the real economy and inflationary impact of the dollar's rise on Germany is a complete red herring," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
"The Bundesbank just does not like what its sees as FX instability and volatility. It is not the level of the dollar."
The next German import price inflation data will be closely watched by the market nonetheless, traders said.

Elsewhere, the dollar was underpinned by continued buoyancy in U.S. stocks and bonds. The Dow Jones Industrial Average index of leading U.S. stocks was up a further 30 points in early trade today and just shy of record intraday highs above 7,000. This week's U.S. Treasury quarterly refunding has all gone according to plan, analysts said, with the final leg later today selling $10 billion of 30-year bonds.
The latest U.S. economic data was in line with expectations, meantime, showing a 0.6 percent rise in retail sales in January and a large drop in jobless claims in the latest week.
